subject: Maths
title: Mutually exclusive events
subtitle: Probability · GCSE Maths
learning_objective: I can identify mutually exclusive events and use the addition rule for probability.

key_vocab.definition: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time. If one occurs, the other cannot occur.

sections.title: Learning Objective
sections.content: I can identify mutually exclusive events and use the addition rule for probability.

sections.title: Key Words
sections.content: Mutually exclusive events -- Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time. If one occurs, the other cannot occur.

sections.title: Method
sections.content:
Mutually exclusive events have no overlap: P(A and B) = 0. So P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Only when A and B cannot happen together

Key examples:
  ✓ Rolling a 3 and rolling a 5 on one die: mutually exclusive  (cannot get both)
  ✓ P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) when mutually exclusive  (addition rule)
  ✓ All probabilities in a sample space sum to 1  (exhaustive)
  ✗ Drawing a red card and a king are mutually exclusive  (king of hearts is both)
  ✗ P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) always  (only when mutually exclusive)

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
Example 1 – identifying mutually exclusive
  A die is rolled. Are 'rolling a 2' and 'rolling an even number' mutually exclusive?
  Rolling a 2 IS an even number
  Both can happen on the same roll
  NOT mutually exclusive
  Not mutually exclusive
  (2 is contained within the set of even numbers.)

Example 2 – addition rule
  P(red) = 0.3, P(blue) = 0.45. If colours are mutually exclusive, find P(red or blue).
  Mutually exclusive: use addition rule
  P(red or blue) = 0.3 + 0.45
  = 0.75
  = 0.75
  (Simply add the probabilities when events cannot overlap.)

sections.title: Identifying mutually exclusive
sections.content:
State whether each pair is mutually exclusive (Yes/No).

(a) Rolling a 6 and rolling a 3 (one die)
(b) Picking a heart and picking a queen (cards)
(c) Getting heads and getting tails (one coin)
(d) Being left-handed and being female

sections.title: Using the addition rule
Finding missing probabilities
sections.content:
All outcomes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

(a) P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.35, P(C) = ?
(b) P(X) = &frac{1}{3}, P(Y) = &frac{1}{4}, P(Z) = ?
(c) P(R) = 0.1, P(S) = 0.3, P(T) = 0.25, P(U) = ?
(d) P(1) = P(2) = P(3) = P(4). Find P(1)

sections.title: Word problems
sections.content:
Solve each probability problem.

(a) Bag: 6 red, 4 blue, 5 green. P(red or blue)?
(b) Die: P(less than 3 or greater than 4)?
(c) Cards: P(ace or king)?
(d) Spinner 1-8: P(2 or prime)?

sections.title: Mixed mutually exclusive
sections.content:
Answer each question.

(a) P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.3, P(A and B) = 0. Find P(A or B)
(b) P(A) = 0.5, P(A or B) = 0.8. A and B mutually exclusive. P(B)?
(c) Three mutually exclusive events with P = x, 2x, 3x. Find x
(d) Bag: 4 red, n blue. P(red) = &frac{1}{3}. Find n
(e) P(A or B or C) = 1, P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3. P(C)?

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
✓ Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time
✗ P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) works for all events
✓ If events are exhaustive, their probabilities sum to 1
✗ Rolling even and rolling a 6 are mutually exclusive
✓ Mutually exclusive events have P(A and B) = 0
